subject: Biochemistry
vignette: An 18-month-old boy has a protuberant abdomen and episodes of early-morning drowsiness. Fasting glucose is 45 mg/dL, blood lactate is 1.4 mmol/L (normal), and triglycerides and uric acid are mildly elevated. Liver biopsy shows glycogen with short, limit dextrin-like outer branches.
question: Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible?
explanation_correct: Cori disease (type III) is caused by deficiency of the debranching enzymes, so limit dextrin-like structures accumulate in the cytosol and glycogenolysis is incomplete. It resembles von Gierke disease but is milder and is distinguished by normal blood lactate, because gluconeogenesis remains intact.

explanation_incorrect.B: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) also causes fasting hypoglycemia but is associated with elevated lactate, triglycerides, and uric acid, and does not produce limit dextrin.
explanation_incorrect.C: Branching enzyme deficiency (Andersen disease) produces abnormally branched glycogen and cirrhosis, not limit dextrin-like structures with mild hypoglycemia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease) affects skeletal muscle only and does not cause hepatomegaly or fasting hypoglycemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency (Pompe disease) causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia, not hepatic limit dextrin.

educationalObjective: Cori disease (debranching enzyme deficiency) mimics von Gierke disease but is milder and features normal blood lactate with limit dextrin accumulation.
